ne-3da316f2.stem: A right-handed 62-year-old understands what is said to them after a stroke, but their speech is halting, effortful and uses few words. Writing is also impaired. Where is the lesion most likely?
options: Upper part of the left precentral gyrus
Left inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area, BA 44–45)
Posterior part of the left superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area)
ne-3da316f2.explanation: Broca's (motor/expressive) aphasia follows damage to the pars opercularis and triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere: speech is non-fluent, comprehension relatively preserved. It is usually caused by occlusion of the upper division of the MCA and may come with contralateral face–arm weakness.
notes: It is the motor area of the leg.
It causes fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension.
Non-dominant hemisphere; it affects the melody of speech (prosody).

ne-63b5b117.stem: After a stroke a patient speaks fluently but meaninglessly, uses made-up words and does not understand simple commands; they are unaware of their errors. Where is the lesion?
options: Posterior part of the left superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area, BA 22)
ne-63b5b117.explanation: In Wernicke's (sensory/receptive) aphasia speech is fluent but its content is disturbed (paraphasias, neologisms); comprehension and repetition are impaired. The lesion lies in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

ne-41911115.stem: In the type of aphasia with fluent speech and good comprehension but clearly impaired repetition, where is the damage?
options: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
ne-41911115.explanation: Conduction aphasia results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas (mostly at the level of the supramarginal gyrus). Comprehension and fluency are preserved, repetition is impaired.

ne-14b513ee.stem: A patient has sudden marked weakness and sensory loss in the left leg; the arm and face are relatively spared. Which artery is occluded?
ne-14b513ee.explanation: The motor and sensory area of the leg and foot lies in the paracentral lobule on the medial surface of the hemisphere and is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. ACA occlusion therefore affects mainly the opposite leg, whereas MCA occlusion mainly affects the face and arm.

ne-01618983.stem: A right-handed 65-year-old has marked weakness and sensory loss of the right face and arm with a speech disorder; the leg is less affected. Which artery is occluded?
ne-01618983.explanation: The MCA supplies the lateral surface of the hemisphere, and so the motor and sensory areas of the face and arm and, in the dominant hemisphere, the language areas. Left MCA occlusion causes right face- and arm-predominant hemiparesis, hemihypaesthesia and aphasia.

ne-b32e3978.stem: What is the typical visual field defect in posterior cerebral artery occlusion?
options: Blindness of one eye on the same side
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
ne-b32e3978.explanation: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe (the primary visual cortex). Its occlusion causes a homonymous hemianopia of the opposite visual field; because the occipital pole representing the macula also receives collaterals from the MCA, central vision is usually spared.

ne-950a7863.stem: Where is the primary visual cortex (Brodmann 17)?
options: On the inferior surface of the frontal lobe
In the occipital lobe on either side of the calcarine sulcus
ne-950a7863.explanation: The primary visual cortex lies on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, in the upper (cuneus) and lower (lingual gyrus) lips of the calcarine sulcus. The upper lip represents the lower visual field and the lower lip the upper visual field.

ne-3b3c0c08.stem: Where is the primary auditory cortex (Brodmann 41–42)?
options: Lower end of the precentral gyrus
ne-3b3c0c08.explanation: The primary auditory area lies in the floor of the lateral sulcus, in the transverse temporal (Heschl's) gyri on the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus. Because input from each ear is represented on both sides, one-sided cortical damage does not cause deafness.

ne-87c1b640.stem: Which Brodmann areas correspond to the primary somatosensory cortex?
ne-87c1b640.explanation: The postcentral gyrus receives touch, pain, temperature and proprioception from the opposite half of the body and is organised somatotopically (sensory homunculus). Its input comes from the VPL and VPM nuclei of the thalamus.

ne-2daff929.stem: In Gerstmann syndrome – agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left–right confusion – where is the lesion?
options: Superior parietal lobule of the non-dominant hemisphere
Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
Angular gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
ne-2daff929.explanation: Gerstmann syndrome follows lesions of the angular gyrus in the lower part of the dominant (usually left) parietal lobe. Damage to the non-dominant parietal lobe instead causes neglect of the opposite side (hemineglect) and apraxias.

ne-28eb07b3.stem: After a right hemisphere stroke a patient eats only the right half of their meal, does not notice people on their left and says their left arm is not theirs. Which lobe is affected?
ne-28eb07b3.explanation: Neglect of the opposite side (hemispatial neglect) and anosognosia occur most often with lesions of the non-dominant (right) parietal lobe, because the right hemisphere attends to both halves of space whereas the left attends mainly to the right half.

ne-dbe702a4.stem: Personality change, inappropriate behaviour and impaired planning and judgement are seen most with damage to which region?
ne-dbe702a4.explanation: The prefrontal cortex is responsible for executive functions, social behaviour and personality. Patients with frontal lobe damage may show apathy or impulsivity, perseveration and socially inappropriate behaviour.

ne-3de004e8.stem: Which lobe is regarded as the cortical centre for taste and is involved in visceral sensation?
ne-3de004e8.explanation: The insula is the lobe hidden deep in the lateral sulcus beneath the opercula. Its anterior part contains the primary gustatory cortex; it is also linked to pain, visceral sensation and autonomic responses. It is supplied by branches of the MCA.

ne-f34b6253.stem: Which structure is essential for transferring new information into long-term memory and undergoes early atrophy in Alzheimer's disease?
ne-f34b6253.explanation: The hippocampus lies in the medial temporal lobe, in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. Bilateral damage causes anterograde amnesia. It is part of the Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary body → anterior thalamus → cingulate gyrus → hippocampus.

ne-1b940b7b.stem: Which of the following is NOT expected in Klüver–Bucy syndrome caused by bilateral damage to the amygdala?
ne-1b940b7b.explanation: The amygdala is the centre of fear and emotional learning. After bilateral medial temporal damage fear and aggression decrease and the patient becomes docile; hyperorality, hypersexuality and visual agnosia appear.

ne-afbdd4fd.stem: What is the largest commissure linking the two cerebral hemispheres?
ne-afbdd4fd.explanation: The corpus callosum is a bridge of white matter containing about 200 million axons; it has a rostrum, genu, body and splenium. When it is cut ('split brain') the transfer of information between the two hemispheres is disrupted.

ne-b72d492f.stem: A hypertensive patient has a sudden pure motor hemiparesis affecting the face, arm and leg equally on the opposite side; sensation, vision and speech are normal. Where is the lacunar infarct most likely?
options: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
ne-b72d492f.explanation: The corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres run very close together in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, so even a small infarct affects the face, arm and leg of the opposite side equally. This region is supplied by the lenticulostriate branches of the MCA, which are vulnerable in hypertension.

ne-46d5bedc.stem: Where are the dopaminergic neurons that degenerate in Parkinson's disease?
options: Pars compacta of the substantia nigra (midbrain)
ne-46d5bedc.explanation: The dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta project to the striatum (nigrostriatal pathway). Their loss causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor. Huntington's disease shows atrophy of the caudate nucleus, hemiballismus a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus.

ne-2a67af34.stem: A hypertensive patient suddenly develops violent, flinging, involuntary movements of the left arm and leg. Where is the lesion?
ne-2a67af34.explanation: Hemiballismus follows a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus on the opposite side; this nucleus normally brakes movement by exciting the internal globus pallidus. Lesions of the basal nuclei produce signs on the opposite side.

ne-e0795ee8.stem: Which thalamic nucleus lies on the visual pathway?
ne-e0795ee8.explanation: The fibres of the optic tract synapse in the LGN; from there the optic radiation runs to the occipital cortex. The MGN deals with hearing, VPL with body sensation, VPM with facial sensation and taste, VL with motor input from the cerebellum and basal nuclei, and the anterior nucleus with the Papez circuit.
